title: biography|a nineteenth-century woman astronomer
text:
Maria Mitchell (1818–1889) was a Nantucket-born astronomer whose quiet determination and telescopic discoveries made her one of the most respected scientific women of the nineteenth century. Raised in a Quaker household that valued education as a matter of conscience, she learned astronomy beside her father, William Mitchell, who calibrated chronometers for whaling captains and observed the night sky from their rooftop. By the time she was a young woman, she could record stellar positions, check navigational instruments, and calculate the paths of celestial objects with a precision admired by sailors and scholars alike.

For years, Mitchell worked as a librarian while continuing nightly observations. On October 1, 1847, she discovered a small, luminous spot absent from her star charts. It proved to be a new comet, later designated Miss Mitchell’s Comet and known today as C/1847 T1. The discovery brought her international recognition, including a gold medal from the king of Denmark. She had not sought celebrity, but the award transformed her public identity from an obscure island observer into a woman whose work could not be dismissed.

In 1865, Mitchell became professor of astronomy at Vassar Female College, one of the first institutions of higher education in the United States to offer women serious access to telescopes and advanced mathematics. She also served as director of its observatory. Her teaching was direct, practical, and deeply moral. Rather than asking students merely to memorize texts, she led them into the dome to photograph sunspots, trace planets, and record the satellites of Jupiter. She taught them that patience was a form of intellectual discipline and that a careful notebook could be as revolutionary as a public speech.

Mitchell’s research concentrated on sunspots, planetary surfaces, double stars, and solar eclipses. She was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1848, the first woman to receive that honor, and later joined the American Association for the Advancement of Science. Yet she understood that professional recognition rested uneasily beside the restrictions placed upon women. She helped found the Association for the Advancement of Women and frequently lectured on science, education, and women’s work. When she received a smaller salary than many male colleagues of comparable standing, she protested plainly. Her refusal to remain silent influenced generations of women who entered scientific fields previously considered closed to them.

After retiring from Vassar in 1888, Mitchell returned briefly to Lynn, Massachusetts, where she died the following year. Her legacy is preserved not only in the comet, lunar crater, and medal bearing her name, but in the students she trained and the principle she lived by: that looking carefully at the universe was both a scientific calling and an assertion of human equality. In an era when women were often praised for charm rather than intellect, Maria Mitchell insisted that the stars belonged to anyone willing to observe them.

title: travel essay|a winter train journey across Siberia
text:
The 076Э from Irkutsk: Borscht at Minus 42
The thermometer taped to the Irkutsk platform read -42C when I hauled my duffel onto Car 9 of the 076Э bound for Yekaterinburg, three days and 3,400 kilometers west. The provodnitsa, Galina Vasilievna, a woman in a wool shawl printed with Soviet-era space dogs, pressed a chipped ceramic mug of chifir—thick, bitter tea brewed so strong it left a brown ring on my thumbnail—into my hand before I’d even found my bunk. “No one freezes on my watch,” she said, nodding at the cast-iron radiator clanking so hard it rattled the window frame, where frost had already feathered three inches thick on the inside of the glass.
My bunkmate was Sergei, a 52-year-old reindeer herder from the Evenki Autonomous Okrug, heading home to visit his sister after selling smoked venison at the Irkutsk winter market. He had a scar slashing across his left eyebrow from a 2019 bear encounter, and he kept a block of frozen reindeer milk tucked in the gap between our bunks, where the temperature hovered just below zero, perfect for storage. By hour two, he was slicing it thin with a hunting knife, passing pieces around the compartment like candy; it tasted like frozen cream cheese, sweet and grassy, with a faint tang of moss.
The world outside didn’t look real. The taiga stretched unbroken, larch and pine bowed under snow so heavy their branches dragged the ground, and the only signs of human life for hours were the occasional wooden dacha with smoke curling so straight up from its chimney it looked drawn on with a ruler, or a snowmobile track cutting across a frozen river. At one tiny, unmarked halt 127 kilometers west of Tayshet, a woman in a valenki boots and a fur hat stood holding a three-liter jar of pickled cucumbers and a stack of pirozhki stuffed with cabbage, holding them up to the window. Galina banged on the glass, waved her over, and traded a pack of filter cigarettes for the lot, passing the pirozhki down the car before the train even started moving again. “Her son works the rails,” she said, like that explained everything. “We stop for her every trip.”
On the second night, the radiator in our compartment gurgled and went cold. Galina showed up with a wrench and a bottle of homemade hawthorn tincture, banged on the pipe three times, cursed the Ministry of Railways for “buying cheap Chinese parts that freeze faster than a Muscovite’s nose,” and had the heat back on in 12 minutes. We passed the tincture around after, and Sergei pulled out a beat-up harmonica and played a Evenki folk song about a reindeer that outran a blizzard, the sound thin and bright against the rattle of the wheels.
I woke at 6 a.m. on the third day as we pulled into a small siding outside Krasnoyarsk, and wiped the frost off the window to see a man in a reindeer-fur coat walking his Samoyed along the tracks, the dog’s breath pluming so thick it looked like a small cloud. The train was running 47 minutes late, but no one in the car complained. On the Trans-Siberian in winter, no one is ever really in a hurry. The cold slows everything down: the trains, the conversations, the way time moves, thick and steady as the chifir in Galina’s pot. When I finally stepped off in Yekaterinburg three days later, my boots crunched on snow that squeaked like Styrofoam, and I could still taste the reindeer milk on my tongue. (Word count: 498)

title: journalism / narrative non-fiction|a town's struggle after its only factory closes
text:
The Last Whistle: Chapter 3 – Empty Parking Lots

The first thing I noticed when I drove back into town on that Tuesday morning in October was the silence. For thirty-two years, the hum of the Hargrove Furniture Factory had been the background music of Millbrook—so constant that most days I didn’t hear it at all, the way you stop noticing your own heartbeat. But on October 12th, the machines had stopped at 3 PM, and now, three days later, the absence sat over Main Street like fog.

I pulled into the diner parking lot, my tires crunching over gravel that used to be packed bumper-to-bumper at shift change. At seven in the morning, this place would normally be alive: guys in grease-stained work boots piling into pickup trucks, coffee cups balanced on dashboards, the smell of sawdust and exhaust mixing with the bacon from Mabel’s grill. Today, there were three cars. One was Mabel’s. One was mine. The third belonged to Tom Reyes, who’d run the factory’s shipping dock for twenty-seven years.

He was already in the back booth when I walked in, stirring a coffee he hadn’t drunk. Mabel gave me a look over the counter—half warning, half pity—and poured me my usual without asking.

“Figured you’d show up,” Tom said when I sat down. He looked smaller than I remembered. His shoulders, always squared from lifting crates, had curved inward like an old bookshelf. “Everyone wants to talk about the ‘story’ now.”

I didn’t argue. I’d grown up here, sat next to Tom’s daughter in homeroom, bought my first real dresser from the factory outlet with money I’d mowing lawns. But that didn’t change the fact that I was a reporter now, and the story was sitting across from me in a frayed flannel shirt.

“What happened in there Friday?” I asked.

He pulled a folded piece of paper from his pocket—the termination letter, printed on corporate letterhead from an office in Chicago. *Due to restructuring and ongoing market pressures*, it said. *Your last day of employment will be October 12. Your final paycheck, including accrued PTO, will be mailed within 14 days.*

“Two weeks’ notice? Nah. They brought us all into the break room at 2:45. Security at the doors, like we were gonna steal a table saw. Lady from HR read off a script. Said the plant’s ‘consolidating operations’ down to North Carolina. Then she handed us these and told us to clear out our lockers by four.” He laughed, but there was no humor in it. “I trained half the guys down in that North Carolina plant. Spent three weeks there in ’19, showing ’em how we do the oak finishing. Guess I trained my own replacement.”

Mabel brought over a plate of eggs, even though I hadn’t ordered. “On the house,” she said quietly, and moved away to wipe down an already clean counter. She’d confided in me the night before, over the phone, that her breakfast receipts were down sixty percent since the closure announcement in August. “They don’t say it,” she’d told me, “but folks are choosing between coffee and their electric bill. I can’t blame ’em.”

Outside, a pickup truck rumbled past, then slowed. The driver—Jake Morrison, I thought, who’d worked in the mill room—glanced through the diner window, then kept going. Six months ago, he’d have pulled in, loud and joking, arguing football with whoever was at the counter.

“My boy’s in his last year at state,” Tom said, staring into his coffee. “Me and Linda had it figured. One more year of overtime, we’d have his tuition paid. Now…” He trailed off. “I’m fifty-three. Who’s gonna hire a fifty-three-year-old guy who only knows furniture? The Walmart distribution center’s forty minutes away, and they’re paying half what I made. Commute’ll eat that up anyway.”

I’d seen the numbers at the county clerk’s office the day before. Hargrove hadn’t just been the only factory in town—it had employed four hundred and twelve people, nearly a quarter of Millbrook’s working population. The hardware store, the diner, the two bars on Main, the little dress shop where my aunt used to work—all of them existed in the factory’s orbit. When the workers stopped getting paychecks, the whole town would stop getting paid. That was the math no corporate restructuring memo mentioned.

“What do people do now?” I asked.

Tom folded the letter back into his pocket and finally looked at me. His eyes were tired, red-rimmed, but there was something hard in them too—the same look I’d seen on my dad’s face when the farm flooded in ’07.

“Same thing people always do,” he said. “We get up. We drink bad coffee. And we try to figure out if there’s a way out of this town that doesn’t mean leaving every damn thing we know behind.”

Outside, the wind picked up, rattling the diner windows. Somewhere, no whistle blew.

title: healthy eating guide|why whole grains and legumes should replace processed snacks
text:
When mid-afternoon hunger strikes, the vending machine’s array of chips, granola bars, and cheese puffs often feels like the easiest fix, but those ultra-processed snacks set off a cycle of energy crashes, nagging cravings, and long-term health risks that whole grains and legumes can break entirely. The first key difference lies in how these foods interact with your body’s blood sugar regulation. Processed snacks are almost always made with refined grains stripped of their fibrous bran and nutrient-dense germ, leaving only starchy endosperm that breaks down into glucose within minutes of hitting your stomach. That quick spike in blood sugar triggers a flood of insulin to clear the excess sugar from your bloodstream, which leads to the all-too-familiar crash an hour or two later, leaving you reaching for another sugary or salty pick-me-up before dinner even rolls around. Whole grains and legumes, by contrast, come packaged with their full complement of soluble and insoluble fiber, which slows digestion to a steady, gradual pace. A half-cup of roasted chickpeas, a small bowl of air-popped popcorn (a true whole grain), or a slice of sprouted grain toast with mashed lentil spread delivers glucose to your bloodstream at a slow, even rate, keeping energy steady for three to four hours without the jarring peaks and valleys that derail focus and mood.

Beyond stable energy, the fiber in whole grains and legumes feeds the beneficial bacteria in your gut microbiome, which plays a far larger role in overall health than many people realize. Processed snacks often contain emulsifiers, added sugars, and refined oils that disrupt that gut balance, feeding inflammatory bacterial strains that contribute to everything from bloating and brain fog to long-term risks of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The prebiotic fiber in oats, barley, farro, black beans, lentils, and split peas acts as fuel for the good bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, compounds that reduce systemic inflammation, support immune function, and even help regulate hunger hormones like ghrelin and leptin so you don’t end up overeating later in the day. Those whole food options also deliver a dense mix of micronutrients that processed snacks strip out during manufacturing: magnesium for muscle and nerve function, B vitamins that support energy production at the cellular level, plant-based iron that prevents fatigue, and zinc that supports immune health, all in forms your body can absorb far better than the isolated synthetic vitamins added to many “healthy” processed snack bars to make up for what processing removed.

Many people avoid swapping processed snacks for whole grains and legumes because they assume these options take too much prep, but they are far more convenient than they seem. A big batch of crispy roasted chickpeas tossed with paprika and garlic can sit in a desk drawer for a full week without spoiling, pre-cooked lentils can be tossed with a little olive oil and lemon for a quick savory bite in under two minutes, and plain air-popped popcorn can be made in a paper bag in the microwave in three minutes without the added artificial flavors and trans fats found in pre-popped varieties. Over time, making this swap doesn’t just cut out the excess sodium, added sugars, and empty calories that come with processed snacks—it retrains your taste buds to appreciate subtle, nutty, earthy flavors instead of craving the hyper-palatable, over-salted, over-sweetened profiles engineered to make you eat more than you need. Even small, consistent swaps, like trading a bag of pretzels for a handful of spiced edamame or a processed granola bar for a small serving of cooked farro tossed with cinnamon, add up to better long-term metabolic health, more consistent daily energy, and a more balanced relationship with snacking that doesn’t leave you fighting cravings every few hours. title: memoir|a diplomat's first posting abroad during the Cold War
text:
First Posting: Vienna, 1961

They handed me my passport in Washington on a Tuesday in August, a stiff navy-blue booklet stamped with the number 2047193, and told me to be on the BOAC flight to London by Friday. From there I'd take the train to Vienna. I was twenty-three years old, had failed my German oral exam twice at FSI, and was assigned to the consular section because nobody in the political section trusted me near a typewriter, let alone a secret.

My apartment turned out to be on the fourth floor of a building on Schmidgasse, behind the Rathaus, with a radiator that banged like a drunken plumber all winter and a landlady, Frau Hoffer, who left notes under my door in a spidery hand complaining about the frequency of my baths. "Einmal pro Woche genügt," one read. Once a week suffices. I was paying 480 schillings a month, about nineteen dollars, and she still thought I was made of money and hot water.

The embassy at the time occupied a building on Boltzmanngasse that we did not own and could not properly heat. My desk sat beneath a photograph of President Kennedy that hung crooked from November onward. I issued tourist visas, notarized affidavits, and listened to a great many Americans explain, with red-faced certainty, that their lost passports were not actually lost but had been "misappropriated by unknown elements." I learned to nod and write down nothing.

Vienna that autumn was a city holding its breath. The Wall went up on August 13th, three weeks before I arrived, and you could feel the change at every border crossing. At Heiligenstadt, where I was sent one gray October morning to observe a routine consular visit, the Soviet soldiers wore coats too large for them and checked my diplomatic passport four times. A junior Hungarian diplomat named Laszlo Kovacs—he told me the name with a small, ironic bow, as if he knew it sounded invented—bought me a coffee in the station buffet and said, "You Americans believe the wall is about them. It is about the ones who wish to leave. There have always been more of those." I reported the conversation. My superior, a weary first secretary named Arthur Denby, read my two-page memo, lit a cigarette, and said, "Porter, never quote a communist over a melange. They say their best things for free and their worst things for the record."

In December I made the amateur's mistake of accepting a dinner invitation from a man named Brandt at a restaurant in Grinzing. He represented himself as a trade journalist, asked gentle questions about my family, and poured an excellent Grüner Veltliner. Two days later Denby called me in, turned a photograph across his desk—Brandt laughing, his arm around a woman I did not know—and said, "His name isn't Brandt. Keep accepting his invitations. Tell me everything, including the wine. Especially the wine." I dined with him three more times. He never learned anything useful, and neither did I, though I developed a lasting preference for the 1959 Loibner.

That winter I also fell in love, foolishly and briefly, with an Austrian secretary named Ingrid who worked at the British Council and skied at Kitzbühel with an ease that made me feel every inch the clumsy American. We went to the Opernball in February; I rented tails for 240 schillings and stepped on her feet during the opening quadrille. By March she had transferred to Geneva and sent a postcard with no return address.

I left Vienna in 1964 older by exactly one marriage—my first, not my last—and by a working knowledge of German that the Foreign Service had somehow failed to give me. I also left with Denby's advice, which I have carried through nine postings and forty years: "In this profession, the things you don't say are the only things you'll never regret."

title: creative writing textbook|writing believable dialogue
text:
Chapter 4: Dialogue That Breathes (Excerpt)
I stood in the campus coffee shop line last Tuesday, eavesdropping so hard I nearly spilled my oat latte. A pair of first-years, bio textbooks splayed across their table, were fighting, and not the polished, punchline-ready fights I’d read in half the undergrad workshop stories I graded the night before.
“You never text back,” the one in the faded Fleet Foxes hoodie said, prodding a matcha scone with her fork until crumbs showered her flashcards. “I sat in the library for forty minutes waiting for you to confirm if we were even doing the lab report.”
Her friend didn’t snap back with a perfectly crafted zinger about being busy, didn’t monologue about her mental health to lay out clear, writerly motivation. She just blew on her iced coffee, ice clinking loud enough I could hear it three feet away, and said, “My mom called at 2 a.m. last night. My grandma’s dog died.”
“Oh,” Fleet Foxes said. She paused, pushed her half-eaten scone across the table. “Shit. I’m sorry. That dog was the only one that didn’t growl at me when I stayed over spring break.”
They didn’t tie up the conflict neatly. They didn’t state every feeling out loud. Half the things they didn’t say hung thicker in the air than the steam from the espresso machine: I was scared you were mad at me, I was too sad to text, I forgot our plans because I was crying over a golden retriever I haven’t seen in six months. That’s the dialogue new writers almost never write, at least not at first.
Here’s the lie I catch myself repeating in workshop, the one I have to walk back every semester: “Write dialogue how people actually talk.” It’s garbage advice, if we’re being honest. Real speech is full of ums and half-thoughts and meandering tangents about grocery lists and the weird guy on the bus who tried to sell you a single sock. If you transcribed a real hour of conversation verbatim, it would be unreadable, the literary equivalent of a security camera feed. Believable dialogue isn’t verbatim speech—it’s speech with all the boring parts cut out, but all the messy, contradictory, unpolished human parts left in.
I learned this the hard way my senior year of college, when I turned in a 20-page short story about my dad and me working on a broken-down pickup truck the summer after my mom left. Every line of dialogue was tight, purposeful: he said gruff, stoic lines about carburetors and responsibility, I said snappy, wounded lines about him never talking about her. My workshop eviscerated it. “Your dad sounds like a Netflix cowboy, not a real guy,” one classmate said. My professor, a chain-smoking poet who’d grown up on a Kansas farm, pulled me aside after class and handed me a marked-up copy. “You left out all the good parts,” she said. “The parts where he stops mid-sentence to yell at a squirrel for stealing birdseed. The part where he asks if you want a lime popsicle three times in ten minutes because he can’t remember he already asked. The parts where neither of you says what you mean.”
She was right. I’d been so focused on making every line carry plot weight, on making my characters say exactly what they felt, that I’d stripped them of the weird, in-between stuff that makes people feel real. I went home and rewrote half the dialogue: I cut the big dramatic monologue where my dad admitted he was scared to be alone, and replaced it with him handing me a greasy rag, pausing for a full minute while he tightened a bolt, and saying, “Your mom always hated this truck. Said it smelled like old french fries.” That one line did more work than three pages of on-the-nose speech ever could, because it was the thing he actually would have said, the small, loaded line that carried all the grief he didn’t know how to say out loud.
There’s a trick I teach my students now, when they’re stuck: once you finish a draft of a scene, read every line of dialogue out loud, and pause after each one to ask: Would a real person say this, if they weren’t in a book? If the answer is no—if the line is too perfect, too explanatory, too ready for a movie trailer—cut it. Let the silence do some of the work. Let your characters talk around the thing they’re actually scared to say. The Fleet Foxes kid in the coffee shop never said, “I was worried our friendship was falling apart and I overreacted.” Her friend never said, “I was so sad I shut down and I’m sorry I bailed.” But both of them knew it, and everyone listening knew it, too. That’s the magic of good dialogue: it doesn’t tell the reader what’s happening. It lets them lean in, close enough to hear the ice clink in the glass, and figure it out themselves.

title: memoir|growing up in a small mining town in the 1960s
text:
The first thing I remember is the dust. Not ordinary house dust, but fine grey powder that settled on the windowsills before noon and sifted through the cracks of our front door no matter how many rags my mother stuffed there. It came from the tipple, from the roads, from the men themselves when they came home at shift change, their faces dark except where the goggles had been. We called it coal dust, but it was more than that. It was the air of Marlington, West Virginia, population 847 if you counted the babies, and everyone did.

My father worked number six seam, eleven at night until seven in the morning. I would hear him in the dark hours, the heavy thud of his boots on the porch, then the low murmur of his voice as my mother heated water on the stove. He wouldn't come to bed until he'd scrubbed himself raw in the galvanized tub, and even then the line around his collar stayed grey. On school mornings I'd find him asleep at the kitchen table sometimes, his head on his arms, while the radio played softly. I never woke him. I'd take my lunch pail and let the screen door click behind me.

The town ran on the company's schedule. The company owned the houses, the store, the pool hall, and the pay office where my father lined up every other Friday with his cap in his hands. Company scrip came in thick metal tokens stamped with our account number, and at the company store prices were whatever Mr. Delany said they were. My mother kept a ledger in pencil behind the flour canister, and I learned early what the red numbers meant. When my father's hours got cut in the winter of '63, we ate a lot of soup beans and cornbread, and my mother stopped buying the peppermint drops she loved.

Still, there was richness in that town, though I couldn't have named it then. Summer evenings belonged to us kids. We chased fireflies in the empty lots and climbed the slag heap until our mothers shouted from back porches. Down at the creek, Jimmy Kovac and I caught crawdads and sailed tin-can boats past the rusted cable wheels. The smell of onions and fried potatoes drifted from every kitchen, mixed with the sulfur from the bathhouse. On Saturdays, men in starched short-sleeve shirts gathered at the gas station to talk union and baseball, slapping the hoods of pickup trucks, while women compared patterns at the five-and-dime.

School was a two-story brick building with a bell that Mrs. Calloway rang by hand. In fourth grade we sat in rows according to our last names, and the room smelled of wax and old steam radiators. I loved the books most of all, because they showed me places where the ground was green and no one's father came home black. Mrs. Calloway noticed. She kept me after school one Tuesday and gave me a worn copy of "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," saying I could take it home as long as I brought it back. I read it under the covers with a flashlight, and for a while the dust on my windowsill seemed like something that belonged only to me.

The worst days were the ones when the whistle blew too long. Everyone in town knew that sound. Mothers stepped out onto their porches, children went quiet, and the men still above ground hurried toward the lift. In '67 there was a fall of rock in four seam. Two men didn't come up, one of them Mr. Kovac, Jimmy's father. I sat with Jimmy on his porch steps while women carried dishes into his kitchen and his mother cried behind a closed door. We didn't say much. We were only twelve, but we understood that the mountain could keep whatever it wanted.

By the time I finished high school, the seams were thinning and families were leaving for Akron, Cleveland, Dayton. My father wanted me to go. He pressed twenty dollars into my palm at the Greyhound station and told me not to look back. I've tried to honor that. But some nights I still smell coal smoke and fried potatoes, hear that porch bell in my mother's voice, and I feel the grit of Marlington under my fingernails. You can leave a mining town. The town doesn't always leave you.

title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
How to Outline a Non-Fiction Book Before You Write the First Draft
If you’ve ever sat down to write a non-fiction book only to spiral 10,000 words deep into a tangential case study that has nothing to do with your core promise to readers, you already know why skipping the outline is the fastest way to end up with a messy, unpublishable manuscript. I learned this the hard way with my first book, when I burned three months writing chapters that didn’t connect, before a veteran editor told me a strong outline isn’t a cage—it’s the map that lets you be creative without getting lost. You don’t need a fancy system or 50 pages of notes; you just need to work through four straightforward steps before you type a single line of your first draft.
Start by locking in your core anchor, the single promise your book makes to the person who pays $28 for it and carves 10 hours out of their life to read it. Skip the vague statements like “this book is about productivity.” Instead, narrow it to something specific: “this book will teach part-time freelance writers how to hit $6k a month without working more than 25 hours a week, using the exact client outreach and pricing system I used to leave my 9-to-5.” Write that sentence on a sticky note and stick it to your monitor. Every section that doesn’t move that promise forward gets cut, no exceptions.
Next, map your reader’s journey from where they are now to where they want to be. Most new non-fiction authors structure their books around their own personal timeline, but readers don’t care about your chronological life story—they care about solving their own problem, in the order that makes sense for them. Start with the gap: what does your reader already believe about your topic, and what’s holding them back from the result you’re promising? If you’re writing that freelance income book, your reader might start out believing they need 10 years of experience to charge premium rates, so your first section needs to dismantle that myth before you teach them outreach scripts. Work backward from the end result, listing every mindset shift, skill, and actionable step they need to get there, and group those points into 8 to 12 logical chapters, each with one clear core takeaway.
Then, flesh out each chapter with 3 to 5 supporting blocks, no more, no less. For each chapter, note what story you’ll tell to illustrate the point, what hard data or third-party example backs up your claim, what actionable exercise the reader can do immediately, and what common objection you need to address. When I wrote my second book, I kept each chapter’s notes on a single index card: if I couldn’t fit all the key points on one card, I was overcomplicating it, or trying to cram two chapters’ worth of ideas into one.
Finally, pressure-test the outline before you write. Read it out loud as if you’re explaining the book to a friend who fits your target reader profile. Do they get confused at any point? Do they ask, “wait, why didn’t you talk about X before Y?” If a section feels like a detour, move it or cut it. Remember, this outline isn’t set in stone. When I was drafting that second book, I swapped two chapters halfway through because I realized readers needed the pricing chapter before they learned how to pitch clients, and the outline made that swap easy—no rewriting 20 pages of disconnected prose, just moving two blocks of notes.
A good outline cuts your first draft writing time in half, eliminates writer’s block because you never sit down wondering what to write next, and ensures the final book delivers exactly what you promised your readers. It doesn’t kill creativity; it frees you up to focus on writing sharp, warm, memorable prose, instead of wasting time digging yourself out of narrative dead ends.

title: journalism / narrative non-fiction|a town's struggle after its only factory closes
text:
The Ghost Whistle of Millford
The first thing I notice when I pull onto Main Street is the silence. For 32 years, my father’s internal clock was set not by an alarm but by the 7:17 a.m. whistle at Millford Precision Parts, a shrill, steady blast that rattled the storm windows of our clapboard house three blocks over. Today, three months after the gates chained shut, the whistle sits rusted on the factory roof, and the only sound at 7:17 is a sparrow fussing in the awning of Mabel’s Diner, where the “OPEN” sign has hung dark since January.

I grew up here, in this town of 1,200 tucked between western New York’s dairy fields and the old Erie Canal. Everyone’s life tangled with the plant: my mom ran the front desk for 27 years; my high school boyfriend worked the night shift to pay for community college; even the Little League uniforms were stitched with the company logo, their red-and-white caps handed out free every spring at the company picnic. The factory didn’t just make transmission components. It made Millford.

Mabel Carter is wiping down Formica counters when I let myself in, the bell above the door giving a tinny jingle that makes her look up, surprised. She’s 68, silver hair pulled back in a scrunchie printed with tiny sunflowers, and her hands—hands that flipped pancakes for three generations of line workers—are chapped raw. “Figured you’d blow through town and not stop,” she says, but she’s already reaching for a coffee mug, the chipped ceramic one she’s kept for me since I was 16 and snuck in after prom.

The diner’s half-empty, and it’s a Tuesday lunch rush. The only other patrons are two retired line workers, Joe and Ray, nursing coffees at the counter, their union jackets zipped up even though the heat’s cranked. “Lunch crowd used to be 40 deep by noon,” Mabel says, pouring black coffee that steams between us. “Guids from second shift piling in for burgers before clock-in, front office ladies ordering pie to take back. Now? I’m open three days a week just to keep the lights on. Can’t afford my line cook no more. My grandson’s over in Rochester, begging me to move in with him. But this place…” She taps the counter, where generations of kids carved their initials next to the ketchup stains. “This place don’t run without the plant. Nothing does.”

The closure came without much warning. Back in October, corporate owners from a private equity firm in Chicago flew in for a 15-minute all-staff meeting, told everyone the line was moving to a non-union shop in Monterrey, Mexico, and that severance would cap at two weeks’ pay for anyone with less than 10 years tenure. My dad, who put in 34 years running the stamping press, got 12 weeks. He still wakes up at 6:45 every morning, sits at the kitchen table in his work boots for an hour before he remembers. “Muscle memory,” he told me last Thanksgiving, staring out the window at the factory smokestack, cold and smokeless against the gray sky. “You don’t just turn that off.”

I drive down to the plant after I leave the diner. The parking lot, once crammed bumper to bumper with beat-up Fords and pickup trucks, is cracked, dandelions pushing up through the asphalt. A chain link fence strung with “NO TRESPASSING” signs wraps the cinder block building, and someone’s taped a tattered union banner to the gate: *MILLFORD PARTS LOCAL 417: 1962–2024*. A handful of cars are pulled off to the side near the guard shack—former workers, I realize, sitting in their front seats, staring. One is Tom Reyes, 47, who started on the line the day after he graduated high school. He’s leaning against the hood of his Silverado when I walk over, holding a can of soda gone warm in his hand.

“I come by most days,” he says, shrugging like he’s embarrassed. “Stupid, I know. But I worked here half my life. My dad worked here. My sister met her husband on the loading dock. Now my 16-year-old’s asking if he can even stay here after graduation, and what do I tell him? I applied to every shop within 40 miles. Nothing pays more than $15 an hour. Mortgage is $1,200. Cobra’s $600 a month. My wife picked up shifts at the gas station out on the highway, but that don’t cover it.” He nods at the plant, his jaw tight. “They took the machines out last month on flatbeds. Sat right here and watched ’em drive away. Felt like watching somebody carry your house out the door.”

That night, I sit on my parents’ back porch while the sun goes down over the canal. For as long as I can remember, the factory’s hum hung in the air after dark, a low thrum you didn’t notice until it was gone. My dad comes out with two beers, hands me one, and sits quiet for a long time. Somewhere down the street, a dog barks. No whistle blows.

“They keep saying towns bounce back,” he says finally. “But nobody tells you how long the quiet lasts first.”

title: teaching memoir|a first year teaching in an underfunded high school
text:
My first year teaching 10th grade English at Westbrook High, I showed up in August with a canvas tote full of annotated lesson plans, a brand-new pack of dry erase markers, and the quiet, untested certainty that if I just picked the right poems, if I spoke gently enough, I could cut through every barrier the world had stacked between my students and the books I loved. The first crack in that certainty hit before the first bell even rang: when I pulled open the classroom cabinet marked “supplies,” I found three crusted glue sticks, a stack of 2008 state test practice booklets with water-warped covers, and exactly 17 pencils, most of them chewed down to the eraser nub. The room’s heat died the second week of October, and the administration dropped off a single space heater with a frayed cord, warning we could only run it for 15 minutes an hour to avoid blowing the floor’s circuit. We kept our coats on through most of November, my students propping their notebooks on their knees because half the desk legs were wobbly, shoving wads of scrap paper under the bases to stop them from tipping mid-sentence.
I cried in my car after the first parent-teacher conference night, when only three families showed up, not because they didn’t care, but because one mom worked two nursing shifts and couldn’t get coverage for her younger kids, another dad was picking up extra highway construction shifts to pay a heating bill, and the third was staying with a cousin after an eviction and didn’t have reliable bus fare to get to school. I’d planned a whole unit on The Catcher in the Rye, checked out a class set from the library, only to find 12 of the books had pages missing right in the middle of Holden’s monologue about the museum. I almost scrapped the whole thing, until Javi, a quiet kid who sat in the back and rarely turned in work, raised his hand and said we could write the missing parts ourselves. We did, for three days, passing the books around, drafting the scenes we thought were missing: Holden stopping for a churro from a street cart, calling his little sister even when he said he wouldn’t, sitting on a park bench watching a group of kids chase a pigeon. Mia, who’d never turned in a writing assignment all semester, wrote a full three pages about Holden sitting in the laundromat watching an old woman fold her sheets, because that’s where she spent most of her Tuesday evenings while her mom worked late.
I spent $127 of my own grocery budget that month on pencils, loose leaf paper, a box of granola bars for the kids who came to first period without breakfast, and a pack of neon stickers to put on finished assignments. I messed up constantly: I yelled once when three boys threw crumpled paper across the room during a poetry reading, then found out later one of them had found out that morning his older brother had been arrested, and the others were distracting him so he wouldn’t break down in front of the class. I forgot to turn in accommodation forms for two of my students with IEPs until three weeks before midterms, and spent two late nights staying after school to help them catch up, their hands chapped from the cold as they scribbled essay drafts, splitting a pack of gum I kept in my desk drawer.
The last day of semester, when most kids bolted for the door the second the bell rang, Javi hung back and dropped a crumpled sheet of notebook paper on my desk before he left. It was a poem about the space heater, about the wobbly desks, about how no one had ever asked them to write the parts of the story that were missing before. I still have it tucked in the front of my lesson plan binder, smudged at the edges, a reminder that the work never was about the perfect supplies or the polished lesson plans. It was about showing up, even when the heat was off, even when the books were broken, even when I had no idea what I was doing. That first year didn’t fix the underfunding, didn’t fix the wobbly desks or the missing book pages or the bills that kept parents from making it to conferences. But it taught me that the things that matter in a classroom don’t come out of a supply cabinet, even on the days you wish they would.

title: self-publishing handbook|choosing a book title and cover that sell
text:
The Self-Publishing Handbook: Choosing a Book Title and Cover That Sell

Let’s get one thing straight right out of the gate: readers do judge books by their covers, and they absolutely decide whether to click based on a title. You might have written the most brilliant novel or the most useful nonfiction guide on the planet, but if the package doesn’t stop the scroll, none of that hard work gets a chance to matter. In self-publishing, your title and cover are your frontline salespeople, working 24 hours a day in crowded online stores and thumbnail-sized search results.

Start with the title because everything else flows from it. A strong title does three jobs at once: it signals genre, promises an emotional payoff, and stays easy to remember. If you write romance, readers should sense heat or heartache immediately. If you write business or self-help, the benefit should be almost instant. Titles that are too poetic, abstract, or personally symbolic often confuse the very readers who would love the book. That doesn’t mean your title must be bland. It means clarity should come first, with style layered on top.

For fiction, I often recommend a short hook title plus a subtitle or series identifier when useful. The hook can carry mood, while the subtitle clarifies the kind of story. For nonfiction, the formula is even more direct: give readers the outcome. A title like “The Quiet Boss” sounds intriguing, but “The Quiet Boss: How Introverted Leaders Can Build Influence Without Performing Like Everyone Else” tells the right reader exactly what is inside. Searchability matters too. Include a natural keyword or phrase when you can, but never stuff a title until it reads like a search engine accident.

Before falling in love with any title, say it out loud, type it, and ask strangers in your target audience what kind of book they expect. Check retailer results, social media handles, subtitles of comparable titles, and possible trademark conflicts. A title that looks clever alone may look confusing beside ten similar books. Your goal is not merely originality. Your goal is distinct recognition within your category.

Now let’s talk about the cover. The most common mistake new authors make is treating the cover like a personal reward instead of a commercial tool. You may adore a certain painting, family photograph, symbolic color, or elaborate font, but taste is not the question. Reader expectation is. Every genre has visual conventions because those conventions communicate quickly. Thrillers often use stark typography and unsettling negative space. Cozy mysteries lean into charm, small-town detail, and hand-lettered warmth. Fantasy frequently uses dramatic illustration and rich atmosphere. Literary fiction can be restrained, but it still needs intentional, confident design.

Study the books already selling in your niche, not to copy them, but to understand their visual language. Look at twenty successful comps and note what repeats: color palette, figure treatment, font style, image complexity, amount of text, and emotional tone. Then ask how your cover can promise the same reader experience while standing out enough to be noticed.

Because most buying decisions begin online, your cover must work as a thumbnail. Shrink your proposed design to the size of a postage stamp. If the title becomes unreadable, the central image disappears, or the colors blend into mud, revise it. Strong contrast, one clear focal point, and limited text usually beat a busy collage. The author name should be legible, but unless you are already famous, the title and promise should dominate.

Hire a cover designer who understands your genre, not just someone who knows software. Give them comparative covers, a clear synopsis, your retail categories, and the exact title treatment. Ask for print, ebook, and audiobook requirements early. A gorgeous wrap that fails as an Amazon thumbnail is not a success.

Finally, test before you launch. Show simple options to a sample of actual readers, track which cover and title combination drives clicks or newsletter sign-ups, and listen to the feedback even when it stings. Selling is not about tricking readers. It is about making the promise of your book instantly visible to the people who are already looking for it.

text:
Chapter 3: The $2.73 Habit That Built a $12M Business
I was sitting across from Javi Mendez at a cracked Formica table in his 1,200-square-foot custom woodshop in 2018, watching him stir a gas station coffee that cost him $2.73 after tax. He’d just told me he was three weeks away from closing up shop. Revenue was $4,200 that month, his commercial saw was 12 days past due on a $1,800 repair bill, and his part-time assistant had quit to take a job at Target with better health insurance.

“I work 11-hour days,” he said, wiping sawdust off his frayed Carhartts. “I answer every quote request within an hour. I stay late to fix uneven joints for free. I don’t get it.”
What I noticed, as he ranted, was that he never wrote a single thing down. When I asked how he followed up with people who requested quotes but didn’t book, he blinked. “Follow up? If they wanted the table, they’d call back.”
I didn’t give him a fancy productivity system. I didn’t tell him to work 12 hours a day, or hire a coach, or drop $2k on a CRM. I gave him a habit so small it felt insulting: Every single day, before he turned on his table saw for the first cut of the morning, he would spend 90 seconds sending one 2-sentence follow-up message to someone who’d ghosted his quotes in the last 90 days. That was it. No more, no less. He could spend the rest of the day fighting fires, sanding edges, running to the lumber yard—didn’t matter. If he skipped that 90 seconds? He didn’t get to turn the saw on.
He laughed at me. Said it was “pointless busywork.” But he was desperate, so he tried it.
Day 4, he followed up with a woman who’d asked for a quote on a 10-foot live-edge dining table 76 days prior. She’d gone with a cheaper out-of-state shop, she wrote back, but that shop had ghosted her, and her housewarming was in three weeks. Could Javi do it for the $3,800 he’d originally quoted? That job covered his saw repair bill.
Three months in, he was closing 38% of those ghosted leads—enough to hire back his assistant part-time, with health insurance. Six months in, he added a second micro-habit: Before he locked up for the night, he spent 120 seconds taking one unpolished photo of a half-finished project and posting it to his Instagram Stories, no filter, no fancy caption, just a line like “Walnut desk for a client in Austin, coming Friday.” He didn’t chase reels, didn’t research hashtags, didn’t hire a social media manager. He just posted one messy, real photo a day.
Last year, Javi’s shop did $12.1M in revenue. He has 17 employees, a 14,000-square-foot facility, and a national waitlist of 18 months for custom pieces. When I emceed the grand opening of his new space last spring, he pulled that crumpled 2018 ledger out of his desk—the one where he’d scrawled that $4,200 monthly revenue number in the margin—and pointed to a sticky note he’d taped to the cover: 90 seconds first. 2 minutes last.
Here’s the lie the hustle bros sell you: That compound growth requires grand, dramatic, life-upending overhauls. That you need to wake up at 5 a.m., grind 16 hours, quit your job, bet on yourself in one big, viral, all-in move. That’s garbage.

title: food-politics book|how industrial agriculture shapes what ends up on our plates
text:
The first thing to understand about the modern dinner plate is that most of it was decided before any shopper walked into a store. Industrial agriculture does not merely produce food; it organizes demand, rewrites habit, and makes certain choices appear natural when they are in fact heavily subsidized, engineered, and logistically enforced. The cheap corn-soy-wheat complex at the center of the field system is less an expression of appetite than an architecture of appetite.

In the United States, commodity programs have for decades encouraged the overplanting of a narrow set of staples. Corn becomes feed, sweetener, ethanol, starch, oil, and an almost invisible thickener in thousands of processed products. Soybeans appear in margarine, dressing, livestock rations, protein bars, and emulsifiers. Wheat, similarly, moves through bakeries, snack factories, and fast-food buns. These crops are not abundant on menus because people independently demand them in every possible form. They are everywhere because policy, machinery, chemistry, and concentrated purchasing make them comparatively inexpensive and extraordinarily versatile.

Livestock production reveals the transformation with special clarity. Cattle evolved eating grass, yet in feedlots they are fattened on corn and soy because those calories can be grown, transported, and delivered at industrial scale. Chickens and pigs are raised in confined operations calibrated around feed-conversion ratios, growth speed, and uniform carcass weight. The result is cheap meat in quantities unimaginable a century ago, but also plate-shaped consequences: select cuts dominate retail counters, nuggets and patties fit mass kitchens, and animal diets compete with human uses of land. The system favors predictability over diversity, throughput over resilience.

Concentration runs through every layer. A small number of seed companies, processors, meatpackers, distributors, and grocery chains coordinate an enormous share of the supply. When buyers demand identical tomatoes every week of the year, growers seek varieties that withstand harvesting, refrigeration, and long transit rather than those with the best flavor. When supermarkets require apples with cosmetic perfection, orchards favor a few visually dependable cultivars. When fast-food franchises need potatoes of uniform length and sugar content for french fries, farmers plant Russet Burbanks and manage them accordingly. The plate is standardized upstream.

Labor also shapes the menu. Harvesting delicate fruits and vegetables remains difficult to mechanize, depending on workers whose wages and conditions are often minimized to keep prices low. Cheap food is frequently cheap because cost is shifted elsewhere—into underpaid labor, depleted soils, contaminated waterways, antibiotic resistance, greenhouse-gas emissions, and declining rural communities. The sticker price rarely presents the full account. A meal built around heavily processed staples and industrially raised protein may look economical while imposing broader public costs in health care and environmental repair.

Trade policy extends the same logic internationally. Subsidized grains can be exported at prices smallholders elsewhere cannot match, undermining local grain economies while creating dependence on global markets. Land in poorer countries may be turned toward export crops—coffee, cocoa, bananas, palm oil, animal feed—while domestic food security becomes secondary. Thus the same plate can contain ingredients gathered across continents, their origins obscured by packaging and branding. Seasonality, once a basic fact of eating, becomes a marketing category rather than a constraint.

Yet the system is not seamless. Its vulnerabilities appear in supply-chain shocks, droughts, fertilizer shortages, animal-disease outbreaks, and farmer protests. Its margins depend on fossil fuels for traction, transport, nitrogen fertilizer, pesticides, plastic, refrigeration, and processing. When energy prices rise, the entire plate trembles. Industrial agriculture has succeeded in delivering calories at remarkable scale, but it has also narrowed diets, reduced agro-biodiversity, and concentrated power.

What people call personal choice usually operates within a designed field of possibility. The carrot can be local and crisp, the fish can be abundant or scarce, the bread can be cheap or costly, but these conditions are produced by decisions about subsidies, land, labor, technology, and corporate concentration. To ask why a plate looks the way it does is therefore not simply to ask what someone wanted for dinner. It is to ask which crops were made artificially cheap, which animals could be raised fastest, which varieties survived shipping, which workers were underpaid, and which institutions had the power to define convenience. Eating is personal, but the plate is political before it is ever placed on the table.

title: personal essay|learning to keep bees on a city rooftop
text:
I signed up for the rooftop beekeeping workshop three days after the city took down the last ash tree on my block, the one that had shaded my fire escape for seven years, its leaves sticking to my window screens every summer like faint green postcards from a world I kept forgetting existed. I was 29, working a remote content job that blurred into a loop of spreadsheets and unread emails, and I’d started measuring my days by how long I could stare at the brick wall across the street before my eyes burned. The workshop was advertised on a tattered flyer taped to a bodega coffee pot, scrawled in neon marker: Bees don’t care if you’re bad at this.
The first time I climbed the rickety metal ladder to the fifth-floor rooftop of the old garment factory in Bushwick, I expected chaos: clouds of stinging insects, the sharp tang of honey, some grand pastoral escape from the honk of delivery trucks below. What I found was Mabel, a 72-year-old retired elementary school teacher who’d been keeping hives there for 12 years, her hands crisscrossed with faint white stinger scars, holding a smoker that puffed like a tiny, sleepy campfire. The hives were painted sunflower yellow and faded sky blue, tucked between raised beds of tomato plants and a stack of discarded rooftop furniture, and below us the city stretched out: laundromat signs blinking, subway trains rattling over the elevated track, a kid on a nearby balcony blowing bubbles that drifted over the fence.
My first month was a study in small humiliations. I forgot to zip my suit closed all the way and got stung on the earlobe, which swelled so large I looked like I was wearing a mismatched costume earring for three days. I knocked over a frame of brood my second week, sending a clump of fuzzy nurse bees tumbling onto the roof gravel, and I froze, certain I’d ruined everything, but Mabel just knelt and brushed them gently back into the hive with her bare hand. “Bees don’t hold grudges,” she said, wiping bee glue off her jeans. “They’re too busy adjusting to whatever the world throws at them. You should try it.”
I didn’t understand what she meant until mid-July, when a heat dome settled over the city, the asphalt holding heat so thick you could see it shimmer above the rooftops at dusk. I trekked up at 6 a.m. with a jug of sugar water, expecting to find hives collapsed from the 102-degree temperatures, the bees listless and gone. Instead, I found them clustered on the outside of the hive boxes, fanning their wings in unison, a low, thrumming hum rising over the sound of a distant siren. They’d hauled droplets of water up from a leaking window unit three buildings over, spread it across the comb, and turned the whole hive into a tiny, living air conditioner. That week I’d spent three nights lying awake panicking about a missed work deadline, about the ash tree being gone, about how none of the small, fragile things I tried to care for ever seemed to stick. But there on the roof, the bees weren’t panicking. They were adapting, finding water where they could, working together, making something sweet out of concrete and exhaust and unexpected luck.
By late August, we pulled the first honey frames, the golden liquid oozing out of the comb thick and warm, tasting not like the clover honey I bought at the grocery store, but like linden blossoms from the trees lining the park six blocks away, like the jasmine climbing the fence of the brownstone two doors down, like a faint, bright tang of rooftop mint that had gone wild in the raised beds. I jarred small batches and gave them to my neighbors, the bodega guy who let me buy coffee on credit when I forgot my wallet, the mom on the third floor who brought me tamales at Christmas.
I still work the same job, still stare at the brick wall some days when my brain feels too tight to hold anything else. But every week I climb that ladder, and for an hour or two I don’t check my phone, don’t think about deadlines or lost trees or all the ways the city feels too loud, too hard, too disconnected. I listen to the hum of the hives, watch the forager bees drift back covered in bright yellow pollen from flowers I never even noticed growing in sidewalk cracks, and I remember that sweetness doesn’t only grow in places you expect it. Sometimes it grows six stories above a busy street, between a tomato plant and a rusted patio chair, tended by a girl who used to kill every wasp that wandered into her apartment, and a group of bees that never got the memo that cities aren’t supposed to hold wild, soft things. Last week I found a single ash sapling growing out of a crack in the rooftop parapet, no taller than my thumb. I didn’t move it. The bees were already visiting it.

title: diet and nutrition book|foods that may slow ageing, with simple recipes
text:
I’m not a doctor, and nothing here replaces one—especially if you take medication, are frail, or have kidney disease, diabetes, or food allergies. Think of this chapter as a practical nudge, not a cure.

 Chapter 7: The Anti-Ageing Plate

Marguerite was 78 when I met her at a community kitchen in Bordeaux. She walked with a cane, complained about her memory, and ate like a teenager in a hurry: coffee for breakfast, packaged quiche at midday, a biscuit with tea. I did not give her a list of “superfoods.” We changed supper.

Within about three months—this is an anecdote, not a clinical trial—she reported better energy and steadier digestion. The dinner that started it? Lentils, tinned sardines, wilted spinach, and a slice of orange. Not glamorous. But it packed fibre, protein, omega-3 fats, calcium, and colour onto one plate.

Ageing is not one process. It is a tangle of inflammation, blood-vessel damage, muscle loss, oxidative stress, and slower cell repair. No food erases birthdays. But a steady dietary pattern may support healthier arteries, muscles, bones, cognition, and skin.

 1. Fatty fish: twice a week

Salmon, sardines, mackerel, and herring provide EPA and DHA, omega-3 fats linked in observational studies to lower cardiovascular risk and possibly better brain ageing. Aim for roughly two servings a week. Tinned sardines count, and their soft bones add calcium.

Sardines on sourdough with parsley
- 90 g tin sardines in olive oil
- 2 slices whole-grain sourdough
- handful flat-leaf parsley
- 1 teaspoon lemon juice
- black pepper
- few thin slices red onion, optional

Toast the bread. Flake the sardines over it with a little of their oil. Add parsley, lemon, pepper, and onion. Eat with a handful of cherry tomatoes. Serves 1.

 2. Beans and lentils: the cheapest longevity food

In Blue Zones research, beans appear again and again in the diets of long-lived populations. They supply soluble fibre, plant protein, magnesium, potassium, and slowly digested carbohydrate. One study in older adults associated one extra daily serving of legumes with slower nutrition-related decline over about eight years, though such studies show association, not proof.

Everyday lentil bowl
- 150 g cooked or tinned lentils, rinsed
- 80 g roasted vegetables
- 1 egg or 60 g grilled chicken
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- lemon juice, cumin, salt

Warm the lentils. Place in a bowl with vegetables and protein. Dress with olive oil, lemon, and spices. This is also useful for sarcopenia prevention: older adults often need more protein than younger adults, spread across meals.

 3. Colourful vegetables and fruit: variety matters

Tomatoes, leafy greens, blueberries, carrots, broccoli, and red cabbage carry different compounds—lycopene, lutein, anthocyanins, glucosinolates. The practical rule is simpler than the chemistry: three colours at two meals.

Green eggs
- 2 eggs
- 80 g spinach
- 1 clove garlic, minced
- olive oil
- 30 g feta
- 1 slice whole-grain toast

Soften garlic in oil, add spinach until wilted, then pour in beaten eggs. Scramble gently. Crumble feta on top. The fat helps absorption of lutein and other fat-soluble compounds.

 4. Nuts, olive oil, and whole grains

Replace ultra-processed snacks with nuts, fruit, or plain yoghurt. PREDIMED, a large Spanish trial, found that a Mediterranean pattern supplemented with olive oil or nuts reduced cardiovascular events compared with a lower-fat advice group.

One-week swap
Replace one daily biscuit with: 15 almonds, 5 walnut halves, or 100 g plain yoghurt with half a grated apple and cinnamon.

Add water. Eat with people. Floss. Food matters, but ageing well was never a single pill—or a single berry.

title: memoir|growing up in a small mining town in the 1960s
text:
Chapter 3: The Smell of Sulfur and Cherry Kool-Aid
The first thing I smelled when I woke up most mornings in 1967 wasn’t my mom’s percolator, though that came second. It was sulfur, thick and rotten-egg sharp, seeping through the cracked window screen above my twin bed, carried down off the slag heap that loomed over our end of Blackpine, West Virginia, like a slumbering gray giant. I was 10 that year, and I’d long since stopped holding my breath against it. The old timers said if you could smell the sulfur, the mine was breathing, and if the mine was breathing, your daddy was coming home that shift.

That June morning, the sulfur was extra sharp, sharp enough to make my eyes water when I leaned out the window to wave at Mr. Torres across the street, who was already hosing coal dust off his pickup before his 7 a.m. shift. He waved back, his face crinkling into a smile above the faded blue bandana tied around his neck, and held up a crumpled dollar bill. “Tell your ma I got that quarter for the eggs later!” he yelled, over the distant clank of the tipple starting up. We didn’t have a grocery store within 8 miles, so everybody traded: our chicken eggs for Mrs. Hale’s rhubarb, my dad’s sharpened drill bits for the jar of marbles Mr. Torres’s son Rico kept stashed under his porch, a pail of blackberries from the slag heap’s lower slope for a pack of cherry Kool-Aid, the kind that stained your tongue neon red for hours.

Rico was waiting for me on the porch steps when I stumbled outside, barefoot, my jeans cuffed above the ankles to keep them out of the red mud that never dried, not even in July. He had a burlap sack slung over one shoulder, and his face was already smudged with the fine black coal dust that coated every surface in town—every windowsill, every dog’s fur, every page of every library book, no matter how many times you wiped it. “Heard the night shift hit a soft seam,” he said, kicking a rusted bolt that had fallen off a mine truck the week before. “Slag heap’s gonna run hot today. We can find coke lumps for the Fourth of July sparklers.”

We cut through the empty lot where the company store used to stand, before it burned down in ’63, its charred foundation still dotted with shards of broken glass that glinted like obsidian in the sun. The company owned everything back then: the houses we rented for $12 a month, deducted straight from my dad’s paycheck, the doctor who came once a week in a dented station wagon, even the elementary school where our textbooks had the names of three generations of miners’ kids scrawled inside the covers. Nobody complained much, not out loud. Complaining got you moved to the houses at the very bottom of the hollow, where the slag runoff pooled in the yards and turned the grass brown.

We climbed the lower slope of the heap slow, watching for the rattle of rattlesnakes that sunned themselves on the warm black rock, until we found the spot where the heat seeped up through the soles of our sneakers, warm enough to make the edges of our jeans curl. Rico pulled two glass jars of Kool-Aid out of the sack, still icy from the spring box he’d stashed them in that morning, and we sat there for an hour, passing the jar back and forth, watching the line of men trudge up the road to the mine entrance, their lunch pails clinking at their sides. I spotted my dad in the line, his hard hat perched on the back of his head, and he waved when he saw me, holding up his own lunch pail—my mom had drawn a smiley face on it with white chalk that morning, same as she did every day he went in.

Some kid from down the hollow yelled that the ice cream truck was coming, the one that drove up from the county seat every other Saturday, and Rico and I scrambled down the slope so fast we slid half the way on our butts, our jeans streaked black with coal dust. I didn’t know then that those were the last good months. That by November, the mine would lay off half the town, that Mr. Torres would move his family to Detroit for a factory job, that the slag heap would slide in a rainstorm the next spring and take three of the houses at the bottom of the hollow with it. That day, all I knew was the Kool-Aid was sweet, the rock was warm under my legs, and my dad had waved, which meant he was coming home for supper. The sulfur was still hanging in the air, and for that day, that was enough.

title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
How to Outline a Non-Fiction Book Before Writing Your First Draft
If you have ever sat down to write a non-fiction book and felt as though you were trying to pour an ocean into a teacup, you already understand why outlining matters. Most new non-fiction writers begin with an exciting topic, a few strong opinions, and perhaps a folder full of notes, then discover halfway through the first draft that their book has no spine. An outline is not a cage for creativity. It is the structure that lets readers feel carried rather than lectured, lost, or repeatedly surprised by information that should have arrived earlier.

Start by identifying the promise your book makes. A non-fiction book is not simply everything you know about a subject. It is a guided transformation for a particular reader. Write one sentence that explains what the reader will understand, become, or be able to do after finishing the book. “This book helps first-time managers give feedback without sounding awkward or authoritarian” is stronger than “This book is about management.” That sentence becomes the test for every later decision. If a chapter does not advance the promise, it may be interesting, but it probably belongs in another project.

Next, gather raw material without trying to organize it too soon. Collect anecdotes, research findings, arguments, definitions, case studies, objections, and practical steps. Use index cards, a spreadsheet, a notebook, or a single long document. The tool matters less than the discipline of putting each idea into movable form. At this stage, do not polish sentences and do not chase missing facts down endless research holes. Your job is to see what you actually have. Many writers discover that their supposed book is really three essays, while others find that a vague idea contains a surprisingly clear path.

Once the raw material is visible, look for the reader’s natural journey. Non-fiction usually works best when it follows the order in which a person needs information, not the order in which you learned it. A beginner may need context before advanced strategy. A skeptical reader may need evidence before accepting a bold claim. Someone in pain may need immediate reassurance before historical background. Ask yourself what beliefs, fears, or misunderstandings the reader brings to page one. Then arrange the material so each chapter prepares them for the next.

A useful outline can be built in three layers. At the highest level, divide the book into parts or major movements. A common pattern moves from why this matters, to what is true, to how to apply it, to how to handle obstacles. At the next level, define each chapter by its job. A chapter should change the reader’s mind or equip them in one specific way. For example, “explain why willpower is the wrong tool for habit change” is a clear job; “miscellaneous thoughts about habits” is not. At the lowest level, list the scenes, studies, explanations, and exercises that prove or deliver that chapter’s point.

Do not make the outline so detailed that writing becomes transcription. Leave room for discovery. For each chapter, I suggest noting five to ten key beats rather than writing paragraphs of planned prose. Include the central question the chapter answers, the strongest evidence, one human story, and the bridge into the following chapter. This gives you direction while allowing your thinking to deepen during drafting. Some of the best non-fiction passages come from connections you cannot see until you write your way toward them.

Build in tension and variety. A steady sequence of claims becomes exhausting, and a long parade of advice can feel scolding. Place conceptual chapters beside stories, difficult material beside encouragement, and broad ideas beside concrete examples. Anticipate resistance, too. If readers are likely to think, “That will not work in my job,” give that objection space and answer it. A good outline respects the reader’s intelligence by showing that the argument has been tested.

Finally, write a one-page outline you can actually see while drafting. Include the book’s promise, audience, working title, chapter titles, and two or three sentences under each chapter. This page is your map. When you get tangled in research or fall in love with a tangent, return to it. An outline can change as your book grows, but until you have a clearer map, change it deliberately rather than wandering.

The goal is not to predict every sentence before you begin. The goal is to know where the book begins, what it must prove, how it helps the reader, and why each section belongs. With that foundation, the first draft becomes less like improvising in the dark and more like walking a path you have already cleared.

text:
Chapter 3: The 12-Minute Audit That Built a $27M Pipeline
I first met Marisol Cruz in 2019, slouched in the back of a windowless conference room at a Chicago industrial supply trade show, picking at a lukewarm chicken Caesar wrap while the keynote droned on about “hustle culture hacks.” She was 38, three years into running her own specialty fastener distribution firm, and on track to miss her revenue target for the third year running.
“Everyone says you have to grind 80 hours a week to win,” she told me later, over burnt hotel lobby coffee. “I’m pulling 72. I answer emails at 10 p.m. I cold call during my kid’s soccer practice. I’m exhausted, and I’m still treading water.”
When I asked her to track every unplanned work task she did for three days, she laughed. “I don’t have time for that.” But she did it anyway, scribbling notes in the back of her beat-up FranklinCovey planner. The numbers didn’t lie: 2 hours and 17 minutes a day, on average, spent putting out fires from orders her part-time warehouse team had mis-shipped the week prior. Another 48 minutes a day answering the same three questions from new clients: What’s your lead time on custom bolts? Do you stock stainless steel? Can you send a sample pack?
She didn’t quit cold calls. She didn’t hire a $100k operations director. She built two tiny, unglamorous daily habits, each taking less time than it takes to brew a pour-over.
First: Every morning, 12 minutes before she opened her email, she did a walkthrough of the warehouse with her lead shipper, Ray, to spot-check 10 outgoing orders flagged as high-priority. No formal reports, no spreadsheets—just a quick loop, pointing at mislabeled boxes, catching wrong quantities before they hit the UPS truck. Second: Before she logged off for the night, she spent 8 minutes recording one 60-second Loom answering the single most common client question that popped up that day, and posted it to a hidden page on her website she linked in her email signature.
That’s it. No 5 a.m. wakeup call. No $2,000 productivity course. Total daily time investment: 20 minutes flat.
The first month, her mis-ship rate dropped 42%. The time she spent putting out shipping fires fell to 37 minutes a day, freeing up an hour and 40 minutes she redirected to checking in with past clients instead of chasing new cold leads. Those Looms? By month six, she had 72 of them, and inbound lead volume jumped 31% because prospects were finding the clips on Google before they even picked up the phone.
Last year, Marisol’s firm hit $27.4M in revenue. She now leaves work at 4:30 p.m. every Wednesday to make her daughter’s JV volleyball games, and she hasn’t answered a 10 p.m. work email in 18 months.
Here’s the lie the hustle bros sell you: that compounding habits require massive, painful overhauls of your life, that you have to grind today for a payoff 10 years from now. The truth is, the most powerful compound habits don’t feel like work when you start them. They feel trivial. You will be tempted to skip them, because what difference could 12 minutes possibly make?
Marisol still does that warehouse walkthrough every morning. Last quarter, she caught a $120k order for aerospace-grade fasteners that had been mislabeled as standard steel, a mistake that would have cost her a client she’d spent three years courting, plus a 20% penalty on the contract. That one 12-minute check paid for every hour she’s spent on that habit, total, for the last four years.
Compounding doesn’t care about your grand five-year plan. It cares about the 20 minutes you show up for, even when it feels silly, even when there’s no immediate win, even when your to-do list is screaming for you to do something more “urgent.”
